sections.report:
**Section.** The whole piece: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Does every element, rule, box, and ornament do a job, so that removing it would lose something?** No. "Export as file" (the text link at about x 314–419, y 316–336) is a fourth choice in a dialog that only asks whether to publish edits to a shared calendar. Exporting has nothing to do with that decision. The viewer has to read and rule out an option that doesn't answer the question, and it sits right next to the risky "Discard changes". That slows a choice that should take two seconds and spreads attention across four actions where three would do. Source: Nielsen heuristic 8, aesthetic and minimalist design: everything on screen should support the main task, and secondary actions that compete with it should be removed or moved down. Fix: take Export out of this dialog and put it in the editor's menu or toolbar, leaving Discard, Keep editing, and Save. If export has to stay here, set it clearly apart from the decision buttons, for example as a quiet link on the far left with space between it and the rest. Kind: convention. Weight: minor. The dialog still works, but it would be faster and safer without it.

**What's working.**
- The headline and body work as a pair. "Save changes to the shared calendar?" names the decision, and "…will be shown to everyone who follows this calendar" tells the viewer the consequence in terms they care about: other people will see it. That is the information they need before clicking Save.
- It hangs together as one thing. One sans-serif typeface, one blue, the same corner radius on the card and buttons, and a soft shadow give it a calm, trustworthy feel that suits a low-stakes confirmation.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** The page behind the dialog is blank and has no dimmed overlay. That may just be how it was captured. In the live product, check that the dialog sits over the calendar with a scrim so it is clearly modal.

Note for the director, not a finding in this section: "Discard changes" deletes the user's edits but looks exactly like the harmless "Export as file" link. That belongs under Interface (destructive actions should look different), so I didn't file it here.

**Checklist.** The whole piece: 8 lines, 7 yes, 1 no (every element does a job)

sections.report:
**Section.** Arrangement and space: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Is every element either exactly aligned with an edge or axis it shares with another, or clearly off it, with no near-misses of a few pixels?**
   - **Where:** The heading and body text start at about x 280. The action row starts later: the "Export as file" label begins at about x 314, about 34 px further in.
   - **What the viewer meets:** The bottom row looks slightly pushed right, as if it belongs to a different column. The cause is almost certainly the link's invisible padding, not a decision. The dialog's other edges are exact: about 49 px of padding on each side, and the "Save changes" button's right edge (about x 1000) matches the right edge of the body text. That makes this one indent stand out more.
   - **Why:** Each element should line up with an edge it shares with another element, and an offset that small reads as an error, not a break (Müller-Brockmann, *Grid Systems in Graphic Design*).
   - **Fix:** Pull the first link's text onto the x 280 content edge, for example with negative margin or by removing the start padding. The other way is to commit to a clearly separate left group.
   - Convention. Weight: minor.
2. **Do only related elements look alike, with no accidental groups or shapes formed between unrelated ones?**
   - **Where:** "Export as file" (about x 314–419) and "Discard changes" (about x 487–621), both on y about 326. They have identical blue link styling, the same size and weight, and sit side by side.
   - **What the viewer meets:** Matching looks make them read as a pair of equal minor options. But one is a harmless side action, and the other throws away the edits to a shared calendar and probably can't be undone. Because the destructive action looks as light as "Export", a viewer skimming for "the other button" can click it by mistake.
   - **Second problem, the gaps:** The gaps along the row don't follow a pattern. From label to label, or label to button edge, they are about 68 px, 42 px and 16 px. The row reads as four items placed one at a time rather than as two clear groups.
   - **Why:** Elements that look alike are read as a group (Arnheim, *Art and Visual Perception*, on similarity grouping).
   - **Fix:** Separate the side action from the decision. Move "Export as file" to the left edge (x 280) as its own group, set apart by a large, obvious gap. Keep the three decision actions together on the right with one consistent gap, and give "Discard" a look that is clearly not a twin of "Export".
   - Defect. Weight: major. The cost is a likely mis-click on a destructive action in a dialog whose whole job is that decision. (The Interface critic may own the styling of the destructive action; the grouping is the arrangement part.)

**What's working.**
- **Padding inside the dialog:** About 49 px on the left, right and bottom, with the "Save changes" button's right edge on the body text's right edge. The panel reads as one carefully made box.
- **Spacing between groups:** About 25 px from heading to body and about 54 px from body to actions. The question and its explanation read as one unit, and the actions read as the answer to it. The eye goes heading → body → "Save changes" without doubling back.

**Checklist.** Arrangement and space: 13 lines, 11 yes, 2 no (exact alignment or clearly off; only related elements look alike), 0 unsure

sections.report:
I finished the walk and looked up the reference entries for the lines I flagged. Here is the report.

**Section.** Interface: applies. It's a confirm dialog with four actions.

**Findings**
1. **Is each destructive action (delete, remove, reset) set apart from the safe actions, so it cannot be hit by mistake?**
   - **Where:** "Discard changes" sits at about x 487–621, y 326, in the middle of the button row. It's one 40 px gap from "Keep editing" and looks exactly like "Export as file": same blue text, no box.
   - **What the viewer meets:** The one action that throws away their rehearsal-time edits looks like the harmless export link. It also sits right beside "Keep editing", which is the option that saves them. Someone moving from "Keep editing" toward the left, or reading the two blue text actions as similar minor options, can lose their work with one click.
   - **Why:** Apple HIG ("Alerts") and Material Design ("Dialogs") both say a destructive action should be visually separated from safe ones and styled as destructive, often red. Desktop save dialogs also put "Don't Save" apart at the far left. Here the far-left slot goes to Export, so the layout drops the separation users expect.
   - **Fix:** Give "Discard changes" its own place, apart from the "Keep editing" and "Save changes" pair. The usual spot is alone at the far left. Give it a destructive style, such as red text, so it no longer matches Export. Better still, offer undo after discarding so a slip can be recovered.
   - Defect, major.
2. **Are rare or advanced options kept behind a visible control, with the main content first?**
   - **Where:** "Export as file" at about x 314–418, y 326, the first item in the action row.
   - **What the viewer meets:** The dialog asks one question, save or not. Export doesn't answer it, yet it takes the first slot in the row. That turns a two-way choice into a four-way scan, and it's the reason the destructive action ends up squeezed into the middle.
   - **Why:** Nielsen, "Progressive Disclosure": rare options go behind an obvious control, and the main choice comes first.
   - **Fix:** Take Export out of the decision row. Put it in the editor's own menu, or behind a "More" control if it has to stay in this dialog. The row then only needs Discard, Keep editing and Save.
   - Convention, minor.

**What's working.**
- There's exactly one primary action. "Save changes" (x 832–1000) is the only filled, bold button, at the end of the row where the eye finishes. The order of importance runs cleanly from filled to outlined to text, so the answer the dialog expects is obvious.
- The title asks the actual question and names what it applies to ("the shared calendar"). The body line then gives the consequence in the viewer's terms: everyone who follows the calendar will see the new times. The user can decide without remembering anything from another screen.

**Couldn't judge from a still.**
- **Focus:** Which button has focus when the dialog opens, and whether the focus ring is at least 2 px with 3:1 contrast. Focus should not start on "Discard changes"; check with the keyboard in a live build.
- **Border contrast:** The grey border of "Keep editing" looks close to 3:1 against white. Its label already identifies it as a control, so this is fine, but measure the border colour to confirm.

**Checklist.** Interface: 33 lines, 30 yes, 2 no (destructive action set apart; rare options behind a control), 1 unsure (focus indicator)
